question: The Commission’s ‘Enjoy, it’s from Europe!’ promotion programme has spent hundreds of millions of euros on campaigns exclusively promoting meat and dairy produce. Some of these campaigns have relied heavily on sustainability claims, many of which are vague, misleading or directly contradict established scientific evidence on the climate and environmental impacts of intensive livestock farming.
Several campaigns reportedly ignore emissions from feed production, the primary source of livestock-related greenhouse gases, or rely on selective data that contradicts total emission trends.

At the same time, the Commission has acknowledged the need to regulate misleading green claims and has warned in its legislative proposal for the Green Claims Directive that intensive agriculture can result in deceptive sustainability messaging. 1.
How does the Commission justify public funding for campaigns that contradict its own green claims work and the EU’s climate objectives, and mislead consumers?
Will the Commission review the programme’s funding criteria and suspend funding for campaigns that use misleading environmental claims?

How will the Commission ensure full life-cycle assessments and adherence to latest scientific consensus on the climate and environmental consequences of livestock farming before approving future campaigns?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.2.2026) The promotion policy1 invests in the long-term competitiveness, resilience and sustainability of the EU’s agricultural sector, and is open to all eligible products without discrimination. Through an annual work programme2, the Commission sets out operational objectives to ensure policy coherence.

This includes requirements for programme proposals to cover at least two areas of action for the climate, the environment and animal welfare listed in Article 31(4) of Regulation (EU) 2021/2115. These actions must also respect Article 31(5), i.e. go beyond the minimum regulatory requirements in each area.

In this context, the policy provides incentives for farmers to move towards higher animal welfare standards and more sustainable production methods. As the Vision for Agriculture and Food3 recalls: ‘sustainable livestock is crucial for the EU economy, viability of rural areas and preservation of the environment and of rural landscapes’.

EU funding enables operators who invest in improving their environmental footprint, to inform consumers thereof and increase their competitiveness. Programme proposals must substantiate all claims made and provide evidence in the form of public documents, examples, quantitative data, etc. in the technical description of the project.

Furthermore, the grant agreement requires beneficiaries to ensure that communication or dissemination activities contain factually accurate information. Finally, promotion campaigns must respect applicable legislation, including on consumer protection, and advertising standards.
1 Regulation (EU) No 1144/2014. 2 Adopted as a Commission Implementing Decision, e.g. C(2025) 8551 final. 3 COM(2025) 75 final, 19.2.2025, p.16.
